correctness.rationale: All horizontal bracket-vanishing subspaces are classified using an explicit tensor contraction centralizer lemma valid in every characteristic. An abelian subalgebra is uniquely a graph of T→Z/C, and counting such graphs gives every coefficient without overcounting. Inclusion-maximal subalgebras must contain the full center; centralizer rigidity yields exactly two pure full summands and every mixed line. A standalone checker enumerates full RREF subspace lattices for six prime-field cases and checks both dimensional totals and inclusion-maximal dimensions; Gaussian binomial subspace totals are checked independently. These computations corroborate but are not used as infinite proofs.

originality.rationale: The all-embedded-abelian-subspace enumerator requires classification of every horizontal bracket-isotropic subspace and every lift across the center. Inspected graph-ideal/derivation results, central abelian-factor results, general maximum-dimension bounds, graphical-group conjugacy enumerations and independent-set/cohomology polynomials do not count these noncoordinate lifts. The maximum-dimension formula alone is already implied by independence-number results and is not presented as original in isolation. Semantic-index queries found no exact or dominating formula; this supports, but does not establish, novelty outside checked sources.

value.rationale: The precise natural invariant is the number of ALL embedded abelian Lie subalgebras in each dimension of the complete-bipartite graph family, including noncoordinate and nonideal subspaces, not just abelian dimension or graph-induced examples. The closed formula spans two unrestricted positive dimension parameters and all finite characteristics. The classification distinguishes inclusion-maximal versus maximum-dimensional subalgebras: an arbitrarily large gap and a substantial projective family of smaller maximal subalgebras, answering an intrinsic subgroup/subalgebra incidence question. These are not merely fixed small tables, an arbitrary slice, or repetition of a known ideal census.
